quote: I can’t recall ever seeing anyone claim that a GLUT is conscious. (Admittedly my reading in this area is not up to professional grade; feel free to correct me.)
content: Nobody claims it, because the GLUT was invented as a reductio. Block’s “Psychologism and Behaviorism” (Block (1981)) introduced the machine now called Blockhead precisely to show that passing a behavioural test is not sufficient for intelligence, and the reply the essay works its way toward, that the table’s apparent intelligence is borrowed from the intelligence of whoever computed it, is the standard reply, given in the textbooks (Braddon-Mitchell and Jackson, Philosophy of Mind and Cognition, 1996). The essay’s Follow-the-Improbability apparatus reaches the same place by a longer road, and the road has a fork the essay does not take. If a GLUT that was pulled from the bin by pure chance is not conscious, as the essay concludes, then what makes the difference is not the provenance but the internal organization, which is what Block said; and by parity, a brain assembled by pure chance (Davidson’s Swampman, Davidson (1987); the Boltzmann brain) would be conscious on the sequence’s own reductionism, since it has the organization. The improbability of the object tells you where to look for the mind that made it; it does not tell you whether the object has one. The essay ends by saying so (“there’s got to be more to it than inputs and outputs”), which is Block’s conclusion in Block’s words.

quote: But a quantum device just implements the Branch Both Ways instruction; when you generate a bit from a quantum randomness source, the deterministic result is that one set of universe-branches (locally connected amplitude clouds) see 1, and another set of universes see 0.
content: Everett is again assumed in an essay that has not argued for it, and here the assumption does work: it is what allows the essay to say that “randomly generating” a GLUT is really selecting one from a bin of all possible GLUTs, so that the improbability must have been supplied by whoever did the selecting. On any other interpretation of quantum mechanics the random GLUT is generated by chance, chance is the answer to “where did the improbability come from,” and the essay’s regress ends in the philosopher’s stipulation, which is where thought experiments are allowed to end. The form of the argument deserves notice. “Here is an improbable, functionally specified object; improbability of this kind cannot arise by chance; therefore a mind selected it” is the design inference, Dembski’s specified complexity, and Book III’s essays on evolution rejected it on the ground that selection produces functional improbability without a mind. The essay rules selection out for GLUTs by fiat, which is fair for a thought experiment, and then draws the conclusion the design theorist draws. The right answer to Block’s machine does not need the multiverse or the design inference. It needs the observation, which the essay makes in its last three lines, that a lookup table has the wrong structure to be a mind.

quote: In this line of business you meet an awful lot of people who think that an arbitrarily generated powerful AI will be “moral.” They can’t agree among themselves on why, or what they mean by the word “moral”; but they all agree that doing Friendly AI theory is unnecessary.
content: The improbability argument applied to AI is sound as far as it goes, and it is worth recording what happened to it. The systems that arrived are not “arbitrarily generated”; they are trained on human text and then shaped by human feedback, so the answer to “how did you choose the AI’s design from a huge space of possibilities?” is “by gradient descent on what humans wrote and what humans approved,” and their moral outputs are improbable in exactly the way a cellphone’s philosophy is: borrowed from the humans on the other end of the line, in this case the corpus. That is the essay’s own account of where the improbability comes from, and it makes the essay’s prediction partly right (nobody got morality from an arbitrary optimizer) and its framing partly obsolete (the question became how faithfully the borrowing works, not whether an unshaped process yields values). The essay’s implication that everyone who doubted the necessity of “Friendly AI theory” expected morality from nowhere is not fair to the people who expected it from training data, which is where it came from.
